title: The tilma of Guadalupe
hook: the image shows a pregnant Indigenous woman standing before the sun

segments.voice: Yesterday, private revelation: visions can help people live the Gospel, but they never add to it. Your line was never required. Did you test a story gently and keep what was good? Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

Her hands are pressed together. Her head tilts down and a little to one side, and her eyes are lowered, as if she's listening to someone shorter than she is. Rays of light pour out all around her. Under her feet is a dark crescent moon, held up by a small angel. Her mantle is blue-green and scattered with stars. This is the image on the tilma, the rough cloak of a man named Juan Diego, kept today in the basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City. Catholics tell the story of the roses he carried in that cloak. Today we skip the roses and look at the picture itself, slowly, the way people have looked at it for a very long time. Today's word is the cloak.
screen: `HANDS TOGETHER, EYES LOWERED.` → `LIGHT AROUND HER, MOON BENEATH.` → `TODAY, JUST THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the light and the moon. Catholic readers hear in this image a vision from the last book of the Bible. In the Douay-Rheims, John sees "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet." The tilma looks like that line, painted. Second, her face. Her skin is dark, and her features are those of a native woman of that land, like Juan Diego himself, an Indigenous man. She doesn't look like a visitor from far away. She looks like the people who first gathered to see her. Third, the small detail at her waist: a dark band tied above her belly. Some readers see in it the sign of a woman expecting a child. If they're right, the image is of Mary pregnant. Which means the person the picture is really about is hidden. He isn't on her arm, as in the icon from Poland. He's within her. When Elizabeth greets Mary in Luke's Gospel, she says, "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." The tilma, read this way, shows exactly that moment's secret. Fourth, what she's doing. She stands in front of the sun, and she prays. Some readers say the picture spoke clearly to people who had honored the sun: here is a woman greater than the sun, and she bows her head to someone greater still. And remember yesterday's rule: no Catholic is required to believe the cloak is miraculous. Pilgrims come anyway, to look. This week we sang the Salve Regina, said the Memorare, fled to her protection in the Sub tuum praesidium, met the Akathist, looked at a scarred icon, learned the rule for visions, and now this cloak. Every one of them pointed past her, to her son.
screen: `CLOTHED WITH THE SUN.` · `SHE LOOKS LIKE HER PEOPLE.` · `A BAND AT HER WAIST: SHE IS WITH CHILD.` · `SHE STANDS BEFORE THE SUN, AND PRAYS.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS THE FRUIT OF THY WOMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the image. If you can, find a picture of the tilma on your phone; if not, let today's description stand in. Then go slowly, from the bottom up, one breath for each: the angel. The moon. The hem of her dress. Her hands. Her lowered eyes. Then come back down to the band at her waist, and stay there. Somebody is hidden in this picture. If you pray, you can say the Hail Mary slowly and stop at the fruit of thy womb. If you don't, simply keep looking. The bell holds the time.

The tilma of Guadalupe. Juan Diego's cloak, with its image of Mary as a native woman standing before the sun, praying, and, some readers say, carrying her child. Today's word, and the end of this week.

Your line: she carries him. Today, notice one person carrying something you can't see, a worry, a hope, a child on the way, and make their load a little lighter. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics venerate the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Juan Diego's tilma, which hangs in the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City; pilgrims come to look at it and pray, and copies of the image hang in churches and homes across the Americas.

fork.setup: you're making an image of Mary for people who have only just heard of her son. how do you show her?
options: as a foreign queen on a high throne.
as a woman who looks like them, praying, with a child on the way.
as a figure greater than everyone, with no one above her.
fork.reveal: the tilma shows a native woman of that land, head bowed in prayer, standing before the sun, and, some readers say, carrying her child: she points past herself.

original.note: Latin, from Luke 1:42 and the Hail Mary: the fruit of thy womb.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous painting of Mary.
what it means: a cloak whose image shows a native woman praying before the sun, with a band at her waist some read as a sign that she carries Christ.
what a scholar hears: Apocalypse 12's woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, painted onto a cloak from the Americas.

notes: Editor: fixed 'yesterday's icon from Poland' (Częstochowa was two days earlier); cut 'the oldest prayer to Mary' from the recap (an unsettled superlative, per day 1340); reworded 'the people she came to' so the narrator does not assert the apparition.
Description of the image (hands together, head tilted, eyes lowered, rays, dark crescent moon, angel beneath, star-scattered blue-green mantle, dark band at the waist): confirm against the image.
The reading of the dark band (cinta) as a sign of pregnancy is attributed to 'some readers'. Confirm phrasing.

'Some readers say the picture spoke clearly to people who had honored the sun' refers to readings of the image in light of Nahua religion; kept brief and attributed. Confirm it is fair and respectful.
'Catholic readers hear in this image' Apocalypse 12: confirm phrasing.
Avoids repeating days 83 and 636 (the roses, 'am I not here'), and gives no date for the apparition.

Week-end recap names days 1338–1343 by the index (Salve Regina, Memorare, the oldest Marian prayer, the Akathist, Częstochowa, private revelation); those scripts were not on disk when this was written.
